items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › SWEDEN statistical research plan
items.text:
Statistical audit, 2026-10-21, of `origin/main` at `4cf7d191` (after PR #77, the SWEDEN repairs,
and PR #78, the medallion hardening). Nothing here changes code, data or published findings. It
follows [sweden-research-alignment.md](sweden-research-alignment.md) and
[sweden-research-roadmap.md](sweden-research-roadmap.md) and only repeats their findings where the
repairs left something open.

The question throughout is what the data can legitimately show, and where the statistical
representation and the social reality part ways.

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › Evidence and provenance
items.text:
| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [pub] | Read from a committed file under `frontend/public/data/sweden/`. |
| [src] | Read from the cited source line at `4cf7d191`. |
| [b] | `tmp/b_check.py` over `language/trends.json`. |
| [cx] | `tmp/cx_check.py` over `similarity/*.json` and `connections/connections.json`. Seeds 20261021, 7, 11; log in `tmp/cx_check.log`. |
| [d] | `tmp/d_check.py` over `belonging/municipalities.json`; log in `tmp/d_check.log`. |
| [e] | `tmp/e_check.py` over `futures/trends.json`; log in `tmp/e_check.log`. |
| [wh] | Read-only DuckDB queries over the shared warehouse: `warehouse/cluster_lab/public-topics-2026-10-12/sources/mart_municipality_year_panel.parquet` and `warehouse/features/sweden/futures_theses/*.parquet`. |

The scripts live in this worktree's ignored `tmp/` and read committed JSON with numpy, scipy and
scikit-learn already installed. The shared `warehouse/portfolio.duckdb` is a 7.6 MB file without
the SWEDEN gold schemas, so no gold mart was queried. The Graphify graph sits in a sibling
worktree and returned no SWEDEN nodes; source lookup was targeted.

Each proposal is marked with what it needs:

- supported: the repository already has the data and most of the code
- verify: something has to be checked before the analysis is trusted
- new data: an ingestion or recount the repository does not yet do

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › A. Politics of Measurement
items.text:
| Item | Finding |

|---|---|

| Question | How SCB's table catalogue and Kolada's KPI catalogue distribute over 13 research domains. |

| Unit, n | One SCB table (4,270) or one Kolada KPI (5,860); 10,130 rows in `measurement/items.json` [pub]. These are different units, so one table is not one indicator. |

| Method | Single-label mapping by SCB subject code and Kolada operating area (`platform/seeds/sweden/*.csv`), then counts. Descriptive. |

| Repairs held | Claims are now limited to SCB (`products.ts:72`); spirituality's zero is described as structural (`Measurement.tsx:166`, `:595`). |

| Open: classification artefact | Kolada's trust KPI U01413 ("avsaknad av tillit till andra") and mental well-being KPI U01473 sit in `health`, because the mapping follows the Kolada area "Hälso- och sjukvård" [pub, `items.json`]. Kolada therefore shows 0 KPIs for `wellbeing` and for `social_relationships` [pub, `summary.json`], while the same platform uses those two KPIs as municipal well-being and trust measures (`platform/models/gold/welfare/serving/mart_municipality_year_panel.sql:9-10`). A keyword pass finds 16 Kolada items matching well-being terms (8 in health, 8 in economy) and 22 Kolada library KPIs in culture [own query over `items.json`]. The zeros and the health count both depend on the mapping. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › A. Politics of Measurement
items.text:
| Open: Porter verdict | `Measurement.tsx:577` prints `supports` whenever economy or employment has the most SCB tables and the most sub-annual tables. No other result is possible for a national statistics office, so the check cannot fail and tests nothing. |

| Ecological or causal risk | Low. The page already says that a count shows availability, not importance (`Measurement.tsx:6-8`). |

| Evidence class | Descriptive. Correctly labelled. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › B. The Ideal Human
items.text:
| Item | Finding |

|---|---|

| Question | How the vocabulary of personal traits in Swedish job ads changed, 2006–2026. |

| Unit, n | Distinct ad text per archive; 23 archives, 8,736,050 distinct texts [pub, `language/coverage.json`]. Near-census, so sampling error is negligible. Measurement error (lexicon, denominator, composition) dominates. |

| Method | Regex lexicon of nine categories (`platform/seeds/sweden_language/ad_language_terms.csv`); matches per 1,000 words with the occupation-field mix fixed at its pooled share; single least-squares break. |

| Repairs held | Changes now end at the last complete year (2025); verdicts must agree across baselines 2008, 2010 and 2012 (`languageChange.ts:15-22`); the 2020–23 field labels are crosswalked (`occupation_field_crosswalk.csv`). |

| Open: denominator decides the sign | Ads grew from 177 words (2008) to 445 (2025) [b]. Every category is used by a larger share of ads (competence +29 %, passion +245 %, stress +42 %, mix fixed), and six of nine fall per 1,000 words [b]. Per-word normalisation assumes mentions grow in proportion to length. A requirement that is stated once per ad, such as a degree or a driving licence, breaks that assumption. Neither denominator is neutral. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › B. The Ideal Human
items.text:
| Open: human-capital verdict | Competence per 1,000 words changes by −17.1 %, −18.6 % and −12.4 % from the three baselines [b], so `Language.tsx:631` returns `challenges`. In share-of-ads terms the same category rises 29 %. The verdict follows from the choice of denominator. |

| Open: personal mean | The mean personal change is +12.6 %, +4.5 % and +3.3 % by baseline; without passion it is −1.5 %, −5.0 % and −3.6 % [b]. One category carries the result. The published verdict comes out `undetermined`, which is correct. `passion` still contains `engage\w*` (`ad_language_terms.csv`), which was 75 % of passion matches in a 2025 shard [alignment doc, B `q5.py`]. |

| Open: breaks | See E. A best single split of a straight line explains 75.2 % of its variance [e]; competence's published 0.772 is at that level. |

| Composition | Occupation field (21 groups) is fixed. Employer, staffing-agency share, SSYK-4 occupation and ad platform are not. County is null 2006–2019. |

| Evidence class | Descriptive. Correct, though the verdicts read as tests of theory. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › C. The Invisible Sweden
items.text:
| Item | Finding |

|---|---|

| Question | Which municipalities are socially similar despite distance. |

| Unit, n | Municipality; 280 of 290 analysed, 10 excluded for a missing indicator [pub]. |

| Method | 12 standardised indicators; Euclidean nearest neighbours in 12-D; PCA to 4 components; K-means k = 2 (gap rule) and k = 4 shown. |

| Repairs held | Random-partner baseline and 1,000 profile permutations: 72 of 280 nearest neighbours share a county against 20.5 expected, 0 of 1,000 shuffles reach it [pub, `municipalities.json` `summary.county_null`]. Turnout carries its 2022 reference year. The source line credits own processing. |

| Open: wrong null for clusters | The published silhouette null shuffles each column independently (`groups.json` `permutation.note`). That removes the correlation between indicators, and PC1 alone holds 40 % of the variance [pub]. The test therefore asks whether the indicators correlate, which is already known. A Gaussian null with the observed covariance is stricter. Its 95th percentile is 0.287 for k = 2 and 0.240 for k = 4, against 0.192 and 0.201 for the column shuffle. The observed 0.352 and 0.274 still exceed every Gaussian draw (100 each) [cx]. The page's wording, "a weak structure", holds; the null it cites is too lenient. Skewed marginals could still produce the excess, so a Gaussian-copula null with empirical marginals is the next check. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › C. The Invisible Sweden
items.text:
| Open: centre–periphery verdict | `Similarity.tsx:590-592` prints `supports` for "Social conditions follow distance to the big cities" from a same-county test. The test shows spatial clustering. It does not measure distance to a city, as the limits text at `:601` says itself. |

| Open: SKR verdict | `Similarity.tsx:611-612` prints `challenges` when AMI < 0.5. The threshold is arbitrary. Four groups against SKR's nine types caps the attainable AMI, and log population and commuting feed both partitions. |

| Feature leakage | Population and commuting are inputs to the clustering and to SKR's typology, so agreement with SKR is partly circular. No outcome outside the 12 indicators has been compared with the groups yet. |

| Reproducibility | Run `public-consensus-2026-10-13` with hash-pinned sources [pub, `groups.json` provenance]; `run_id` and `code_sha` are null. |

| Evidence class | Exploratory. Correct. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › D. Infrastructure of Belonging
items.text:
| Item | Finding |

|---|---|

| Question | Where people can take part in collective life without consuming; measured through public libraries. |

| Unit, n | Municipality-year, 2014–2025, 3,446 rows [pub]. Balanced panels: service points 271, visits 216 municipalities [pub, `belonging/coverage.json`]. |

| Repairs held | 12 zero-visit rows, one zero-service-point row and 6 partial organisation sums set to missing and counted [pub]. The Putnam/Habermas verdict is now `undetermined` (`Belonging.tsx:688`). |

| Open: the decline is mostly the pandemic | In the 216-municipality balanced panel, visits go 53.77 M (2014), 50.01 M (2019), 25.08 M (2021), 40.36 M (2025) [d]. Paired change 2014→2019 is −6.7 % (n 262) and 2019→2025 −19.3 % (n 265) [d]. The headline at `Belonging.tsx:287` puts the 12 % fall in service points and the 25 % fall in visits in one sentence, which invites the reader to link them. Within municipalities, those that lost a service point 2014→2019 had a median log visit change of −0.089 against −0.085 for the rest; Spearman ρ between the change in service points and the change in log visits is 0.079 [d]. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › D. Infrastructure of Belonging
items.text:
| Open: "use follows supply" | Cross-sectional ρ between service points per 10,000 and visits per inhabitant is 0.145 (2025, n 281) and 0.21 (2019) [d]. With log population partialled out it is 0.03 and 0.06 [d]. Service points per inhabitant correlate −0.67 with log population [d], so the association is population size. The reading at `Belonging.tsx:699-710` also says "more people visit them", but a visit is an event at a door counter, not a person. |

| Concepts | Availability (service points), accessibility (distance, hours), use (visits, loans), participation (active borrowers, activities) and belonging (not measured) are separate. Only the first and third are on the page. Visits include commuters and visitors from other municipalities. |

| Evidence class | Descriptive. Correct. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › E. The Lost Futures
items.text:
| Item | Finding |

|---|---|

| Question | How often the Riksdag speaks of the future and with which themes; DiVA thesis abstracts as a second corpus. |

| Unit, n | Speech; 32 calendar years 1994–2025 [pub, `futures/trends.json`]. DiVA: abstracts deduplicated to each record's latest month (`int_sweden_future_theses_latest.sql`); 720,979 record-months for 444,894 records in the feature files [wh]. |

| Repairs held | Session 1999/2000 counted, running year 2026 dropped, words per speech published, DiVA Swedish-only and deduplicated. |

| Open: length | Future share against words per speech: ρ 0.826 in levels and 0.565 in first differences (n 31) [e]. The length link survives detrending, so it is a real confounder and not only a shared trend. `marker_per_1000_words` is still null in every row [pub], so the per-word rate promised by `export_futures.py:8-9` does not exist yet. |

| Open: break statistic | The break reported per theme is the best two-mean split. A pure linear trend gives 0.751 of variance explained at n = 32, and a random walk reaches 0.70 or more in 37.7 % of 2,000 runs [e]. Published values: security 0.739, culture 0.759, alternatives 0.729 [pub]. None of them is distinguishable from a smooth trend or a random walk. Lag-1 autocorrelation of the yearly series runs from 0.32 to 0.88 [e]. FuturesExplore labels it "Most likely single break" (`FuturesExplore.tsx:199`), which implies a probability model that is not there. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › E. The Lost Futures
items.text:
| Open: lexicon vintage | The `alternatives` theme is a list of named proposals: löntagarfonder, sextimmars arbetsdag, medborgarlön, basinkomst, kooperativ (`trends.json` pattern). Yearly counts of future speeches with the theme fall from 76 (1994) to 9–18 (2022–2025) [pub]. That records the end of specific 1990s debates. Alternatives phrased in today's terms (four-day week, degrowth) do not match. "Faded from the chamber's future talk" (`Futures.tsx:192`) reads as a statement about imagination. |

| Open: theme polysemy | `security` contains `trygghet\w*` (welfare security, trygghetssystem) and `stabilitet\w*` (financial stability) beside `försvar\w*` and `gängkriminalitet\w*`. `technology` contains `forskning\w*`; `culture` contains `bibliotek\w*` and every `kultur\w*` compound. The securitisation verdict (`Futures.tsx:556-559`) needs the sub-terms apart. |

| Open: DiVA jump | DiVA future share is 0.121–0.137 for 2015–2023, then 0.162 (2024) and 0.188 (2025) [wh]. Median abstract length stays at 226–234 words, and the rise appears in every length quartile (lowest quartile 0.079 in 2023, 0.143 in 2025) [wh]. Length does not explain it. Candidates to check: generated or template text after 2022, the "framtida forskning" convention matching `framtid\w*`, and changes in which institutions deposit. |

| Evidence class | Descriptive. Correct. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › Connections
items.text:
| Item | Finding |

|---|---|

| Relationships | Visits per inhabitant against post-secondary share, and against median earned income, 2024; service points per 10,000 against log population (marked trivial) [pub]. Two joins rejected with reasons (B×E, speeches×theses). |

| Unit, n, missing | Municipality; n 280 for the two visit relationships. The 10 missing are not C's 10 exclusions. They are municipalities without 2024 visits, including Upplands Väsby, Haninge and Upplands-Bro [cx]. That missingness is unlikely to be random: three of ten are Stockholm suburbs. The docstring calls the panel "SWEDEN C's municipalities" (`export_connections.py:69`) while it keeps all 290. |

| Method | Spearman ρ, iid percentile bootstrap (2,000, seed 20261020), partial ρ after removing rank of log population from both ranks (`export_connections.py:55-65`). |

| Results reproduce | ρ 0.005 and 0.102; partial 0.203 and 0.180 [cx]. |

| Suppression | The raw association is about zero. The partial exists because post-secondary share correlates 0.75 with log population and visits per inhabitant −0.17 [cx]. The finding is conditional on a linear adjustment in ranks. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › Connections
items.text:
| Uncertainty not shown | No interval is published for the partial ρ. Recomputed: iid bootstrap [0.072, 0.328] for education and [0.060, 0.293] for income; county-cluster bootstrap [0.000, 0.354] and [0.038, 0.302] [cx]. Residual permutation p, unadjusted, 0.0006 and 0.0018 [cx]. Moran's I (6 nearest neighbours) of the visit rate is −0.021 and of its partial residual −0.013, so spatial dependence in the outcome is small; education and income have I 0.56 and 0.54 [cx]. |

| Two tests, one question | Partialling income out of the education relationship lowers it to 0.125; education out of income lowers it to 0.083 [cx]. They are one socioeconomic gradient counted twice, not two findings. Adding in- and out-commuting moves them little (0.189, 0.165) [cx]. |

| Multiple comparisons | The page says "several relationships are tested; none is called significant" (`export_connections.py:191`). That avoids false claims, but it is not a correction. The `assessment` rule (`:165-166`) mixes the interval for raw ρ with the point estimate of partial ρ against a fixed 0.1, and both relationships come out `uncertain` although the partials are the better-supported quantity. With Holm over the two, both partials stay below 0.01. The family the rule should cover is every relationship ever considered for the page, and nothing records that family. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › Connections
items.text:
| Pre-specification | `Connections.tsx:107` says each relationship "was defined before it was computed". The export and the first `connections.json` were added in the same commit, `8f7dbcb5`. No dated specification exists, so the claim cannot be checked. |

| Trivial pair | The partial ρ of service points per 10,000 against log population, with log population held constant, is 0.015 by construction [pub]. Publishing it adds nothing. |

| Tests | No pytest covers `export_connections.py` (no test file references it). |

| Evidence class | Exploratory. Correct. No causal language found. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 2. The five highest-value new analyses
items.text:
Ordered by research value against cost. All five use data the repository already holds or
already knows how to fetch.

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 2.1 E: separate length from theme, and test breaks against a trend null
items.text:
- Question: Does future talk, and does each theme, change once speech length and smooth
  trend are accounted for?
- Method: (1) Store marker and theme matches per speech so a per-1,000-word rate exists. (2)
  Report shares within fixed length bands (quartiles of 1994–2025 speech length), so a year is
  compared with itself at equal length. (3) Replace the two-mean split with a linear trend plus one
  break, scored against a null of an AR(1) process around a linear trend fitted to the same series.
  Fit by least squares and use a parametric bootstrap of 999 series (seed fixed). Report the break
  year only when the improvement over trend exceeds the null's 95th percentile. Treat the nine
  themes as one family with Holm. (4) Split `security` into defence and crime, welfare security
  and stability, and `culture` into arts and heritage, libraries and other compounds. Report each
  sub-term's yearly count.
- Supported: the series in `trends.json`, `one_break` in `export_language.py:46`, the
  theme patterns.
- Verify: sub-term counts need the recount; parties.json uses the same denominators.
- New data: a recount of the 32 Riksdag sessions from the archives (the source exists;
  `futures_language.py` needs per-speech match counts).
- What cannot be concluded: frequency does not measure imagination or intent. The Riksdag
  is one genre.

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 2.2 B: denominators, sub-lexicons and composition
items.text:
- Question: Which changes in job-ad language survive the choice of denominator, the split of
  broad term families, and a change in who advertises?
- Method: (1) Publish three measures side by side: share of texts, matches per 1,000 words,
  and share of texts within fixed length bands (2010 quartiles). Call a change stable only when
  all three agree in sign. (2) Split `passion` into `engag*` and passion/brinner/entusiasm, and
  `identity` into the recruitment formulas ("personlig lämplighet", "personliga egenskaper") and
  the rest. (3) Shift-share decomposition per category: total change = within-field change +
  field-mix change, at the 21-field level, then at SSYK-4 where taxonomy ids exist (2023+). (4)
  A staffing-agency indicator from employer name for 2023+, with the change computed with and
  without agencies. (5) Manual validation: 50 matches per category and period, coded by two
  readers, with precision and Cohen's κ.
- Supported: `fields.json` cells, the trends mart, the crosswalk, the JobTech taxonomy cache.
- Verify: whether SSYK-4 and employer fields exist in the 2006–2019 archives; the
  agency rule's precision on a sample.
- New data: a re-stream of the 23 archives to store length bands and sub-lexicon counts.
- What cannot be concluded: how employers select, how work feels, or anything about
  individual workers.

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 2.3 C: sensitivity of neighbours and groups, plus an outcome outside the model
items.text:
- Question: How much of the similarity map is the definition, and do the groups separate
  anything they were not built from?
- Method: (1) Neighbour stability: Jaccard overlap of each municipality's five neighbours
  under five variants (all 12 features; without log population; without the commuting pair; PCA-4
  space; Mahalanobis distance). Report the median and the share of municipalities whose first
  neighbour changes. (2) Cluster null: Gaussian copula with the observed rank correlation and
  empirical marginals, 200 draws, seed fixed; silhouette and gap per k. (3) Temporal stability:
  rerun on 2020–2023 and report ARI against 2024 for k = 2 and k = 4. (4) Out-of-model outcomes:
  2022 party shares (already in `mart_municipality_year_cross_subject`) and the 2024 library
  rates. Report the share of variance explained by group with a permutation null over
  municipalities. Use only variables not among the 12 inputs.
- Supported: the 280 × 12 matrix in `similarity/municipalities.json`, `ml/research/regions.py`,
  the panel parquet, the election and library columns of the cross-subject mart.
- Verify: 2018 and 2019 lack employment, so the window is 2020–2024; turnout repeats an
  election year.
- New data: none.
- What cannot be concluded: the groups are constructions of 12 municipal averages. They do
  not describe residents.

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 2.4 D: what changed after 2019, and where
items.text:
- Question: Is the fall in library visits a slow loss of supply, or a pandemic break that
  has not recovered, and does it differ by municipality type?
- Method: (1) The balanced visits panel (216), with 2014–2019 and 2019–2025 reported apart.
  (2) Recovery ratio per municipality, 2025 visits / 2019 visits, by SKR group, with bootstrap
  intervals for each group's median. (3) A two-way fixed-effects model of log visits on service
  points, with municipality and year effects, as a description of within-municipality covariation.
  Report it with county-clustered standard errors. (4) Missing-data sensitivity: every change
  computed on the balanced panel, on all paired municipalities, and with the 13 repaired zeros
  restored, so the effect of each choice is visible.
- Supported: `belonging/municipalities.json`, SKR groups in `similarity/municipalities.json`.
- Verify: whether door-counter methods changed in 2020–2022 (KB documentation);
  whether staffless (meröppet) hours move visits between categories.
- New data: bibstat opening-hour terms (Open101–106, Open201–206) to add accessibility.
  Same API, small.
- What cannot be concluded: belonging, loneliness or civic participation. Visits are door
  counts, and they include people from other municipalities.

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 2.5 A: classification sensitivity and the "measured elsewhere" check
items.text:
- Question: How much do domain counts depend on the mapping, and which thin domains are thin
  only in these two catalogues?
- Method: (1) A second, multi-label classification by title keywords, with a seed per domain,
  for every item. Publish the count under both mappings and the share of items that change
  domain. (2) Count measures, not tables, from the SCB metadata already fetched for 1,299
  tables. (3) For each domain, list which other agencies publish municipal statistics on it,
  from catalogue metadata only, as a presence/absence table with its source. (4) Split
  `is_current` into ongoing series and projections (`mart_sweden_measurement_items.sql:50`).
- Supported: `items.json`, the seeds, the SCB metadata on disk.
- Verify: Socialstyrelsen and Folkhälsomyndigheten catalogue licences before ingesting.
- New data: those catalogues, metadata only.
- What cannot be concluded: absence from an indexed catalogue is not absence from society
  or from statistics.

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 3.1 C×D matched-neighbour comparison
items.text:
- Question: Among municipalities that C finds socially alike, how much do library supply and
  use differ?
- Why it matters: It answers C's stated link ("access to meeting places within each
  similarity group", `products.ts:92`) without a correlation across very different places.
- Data and keys: `similarity/municipalities.json` neighbours (five per municipality,
  2024 inputs) joined on municipality code to `belonging/municipalities.json`, 2024. 280
  municipalities with neighbours; visits exist for 280 of 290 in 2024.
- Method: For each municipality, the difference between its visits per inhabitant and the
  median of its five neighbours, and the same for service points per 10,000. Report the
  distribution, the share of municipalities more than 50 % above or below their neighbours, and a
  permutation reference that replaces each neighbour set with five random municipalities of the
  same SKR group (999 rounds, seed fixed).
- Confounders: Matching covers the 12 indicators. It does not cover tourism, students,
  commuting into a regional centre, or counting methods.
- Sensitivity: Neighbour sets from the variants in 2.3; 2019 instead of 2024 for the library
  values.
- Alternatives: A municipality far above its neighbours may host a regional library, a
  university or a tourist season.
- Cannot conclude: Whether provision causes use, or anything about residents.
- Classification: Descriptive comparison.
- Status: Supported. No new data.

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 3.2 C panel × D: within-municipality change, 2014–2019 and 2019–2024
items.text:
- Question: Did library visits fall more where population fell, aged or lost income?

- Why it matters: Change within the same municipality removes every fixed difference between

  places, which is the main confounder of the current cross-section.

- Data and keys: `belonging/municipalities.json` (2014–2025) and the municipal panel

  (`mart_municipality_year_panel`: population, income, unemployment, dependency ratio, yearly

  1998–2025 [wh]) on municipality code and year.

- Method: Log change in visits against log change in population, change in median income

  and change in dependency ratio, as one pre-registered model per period. Report coefficients with

  county-clustered intervals and a permutation of change vectors across municipalities. Three

  coefficients in two periods form one family; correct it with Holm.

- Confounders: Library reorganisation, counting changes, the pandemic (hence the split

  periods), merged service points.

- Sensitivity: Balanced against paired municipalities; with and without the 13 repaired rows;

  Theil–Sen slopes beside least squares.

- Alternatives: Shrinking municipalities may close branches first; reverse ordering cannot be

  excluded.

- Cannot conclude: Causal effects of demographic change on library use.

- Classification: Exploratory statistical relationship. It can become a validated relationship

  only if the specification is committed before the first run and a later year (2026 data)

  confirms it out of sample.

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 3.2 C panel × D: within-municipality change, 2014–2019 and 2019–2024
items.text:
- Status: Supported (both panels exist). Verify that population in D comes from the same

  panel (`belonging/coverage.json` says `gold.mart_municipality_year_panel`).

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 3.3 C×D cross-section, re-specified as one model
items.text:
- Question: After population size, is there a socioeconomic gradient in library visits?
- Why it matters: It is the current Connections result, and its honest form is one modest
  conditional association, not two uncertain ones.
- Data and keys: As today: `mart_municipality_year_cross_subject`, 2024, n 280.
- Method: One rank regression of visits per inhabitant on log population, post-secondary share,
  income, in-commuting and out-commuting, all in ranks. Report each coefficient and the partial ρ
  with a county-cluster bootstrap interval. Report the result for 2019 and 2024 next to each other,
  and test the missingness: compare the 10 municipalities without visits with the rest on the 12
  C indicators.
- Confounders: Regional centres drawing visitors, students, door-counter quality.
- Sensitivity: Without the 5 % largest municipalities (partial 0.193 and 0.209 today [cx]);
  with visits per active borrower instead of per inhabitant.
- Alternatives: Education and income are one gradient: controlling for either lowers the other to 0.08–0.13 [cx].
- Cannot conclude: That education makes people visit libraries; individual behaviour
  (ecological fallacy); causality in either direction.
- Classification: Exploratory statistical relationship today. With pre-specification and the
  2019 replication it would be the platform's first validated statistical relationship.
- Status: Supported.

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › Other candidates, classified
items.text:
| Pair | Classification | Reason |

| D × trust or well-being (Kolada U01413, U01473) | Unsupported before 2022; interpretive hypothesis after | Before 2022 the municipal panel holds 19–23 distinct trust values a year, integers from 14 to 41, for 168–219 municipalities [wh]. That is close to one value per county, so a municipal correlation would count county values many times. 2022 and 2024 have 177 and 143 distinct values for 268 and 237 municipalities [wh]. Survey estimates with small samples and non-random suppression; show side by side, never correlate, until the survey's own margins of error are known. |

items.title: docs/sweden-statistical-research-plan.md › 5. Recommended methods and assumptions
items.text:
- Effect sizes first: Every published change carries its denominator, both endpoints and n.

  Relative changes of small rates also carry the absolute change.

- Intervals: Percentile bootstrap with a fixed seed for cross-sections; county-cluster

  bootstrap where the predictor is spatially autocorrelated (Moran's I above 0.3); block

  bootstrap of years for yearly series with lag-1 autocorrelation above 0.5.

- Nulls: Permutation over municipalities for spatial claims; Gaussian copula with empirical

  marginals for cluster validity; AR(1) around a fitted trend for breaks in yearly series.

- Families: A family is all relationships or themes that answer one question on one page.

  Record it in the export before computing, correct with Holm, and publish the adjusted values next

  to the raw ones. Do not use a significance threshold as a verdict; classify by interval and

  direction.

- Verdict rule: A reading `supports` only when the result could have come out against it,

  the direction holds across the stated sensitivity variants, and the interval excludes zero.

  Otherwise `undetermined`. Thresholds such as ±10 % stay as stated conventions, never as tests.

- Denominators: Report text measures in three forms (share of texts, per 1,000 words, share

  within fixed length bands). Riksdag, DiVA and any SOU corpus keep their own denominators and are

  never pooled.

- Composition: Shift-share decomposition for B (occupation, employer) and E (party, speaker

items.text:

- Lexicons: Precision from coded samples with Cohen's κ for two readers; recall from a sample

  of non-matching texts; the version of each pattern stored with its counts. Report lexicon vintage:

  the year each term entered the list.

- Ecological inference: Every municipal relationship says "municipalities where", never

  "people who".

- Missingness: Each analysis states its complete-case n, its balanced-panel n and the

  difference in result between them. Compare excluded units with included ones on known variables.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Symbolic Atlas
items.text:
An experimental subject in the platform: can recurring symbolic meanings be found in
mythology, folklore and literature **without deciding the meanings first**? Every use of a
symbol word in a small public-domain corpus is placed on a map by the sentences around it and
grouped without supervision. The site shows the result at `#symbolic-atlas`.

The MVP proves the pipeline end to end. It does not claim the clusters are symbolic meanings.

The baseline showed the clusters follow books more than symbols, which raised a follow-up
question, investigated in [Deconfounding experiments](#deconfounding-experiments):

> Can symbolic meaning be separated from literary style and document identity in an
> unsupervised semantic space?

Reading the results then exposed paratext (glossaries, indexes) as a second confounder, which
led to [Paratext cleaning](#paratext-cleaning) and a [human review](#human-review) step: the
atlas moves from an interesting clustering picture to a transparent, human-reviewed
investigation of cross-document symbolic context. Nothing here claims a symbolic meaning has
been discovered; a cluster gets a name only when a person has read it.

| Version | What changed | Largest book in a cluster | Cross-book clusters (passages in them) |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | Baseline embeddings | 74 % | 5 of 43 (7 %) |
| v2 | Book-centred embeddings | 57 % | 24 of 50 (43 %) |
| v3 | Paratext cleaned, book-centred | 58 % | 25 of 59 (32 %), ranked for review |

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Flow
items.text:
```
Project Gutenberg ──ingest──▶ warehouse/raw/symbolic        (rawstore: URL, time, SHA-256)
  ──dbt bronze──▶ stg_symbolic_documents                    (text as fetched + provenance)
  ──dbt silver──▶ int_symbolic_documents                    (dbt Python model, nlp/symbolic/cleaning.py:
                                                              boilerplate and paratext cut, audited)
               ▶ int_symbol_occurrences                     (dbt Python model, nlp/symbolic/context.py)
  ──Python ML───▶ warehouse/features/symbolic               (embeddings, UMAP, HDBSCAN, evaluation)
               ▶ experiments/                               (baseline, masked, book-centred, both)
               ▶ review/                                    (rank_clusters.py: candidates for human review)
  ──dbt gold────▶ mart_symbol_atlas, mart_symbol_profiles
  ──publish─────▶ frontend/public/data/symbolic             (summary.json, preview.json, *.parquet → R2)
  ──frontend────▶ #symbolic-atlas
```

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Commands
items.text:
```
npm run symbolic:ingest    # python platform/ingest/symbolic/ingest_corpus.py
npm run symbolic:silver    # dbt: seeds, bronze, silver (tag:symbolic without gold)
npm run symbolic:ml        # python platform/nlp/symbolic/pipeline.py
npm run symbolic:gold      # dbt: the two gold marts
npm run symbolic:publish   # python platform/publish/symbolic/export_symbolic.py
npm run symbolic:build     # all of the above in order

npm run symbolic:clean        # snapshot occurrences, rebuild silver with the cleaning, write the audit
npm run symbolic:experiments  # python platform/nlp/symbolic/experiments.py (all four variants)
npm run symbolic:review       # python platform/nlp/symbolic/rank_clusters.py book_centered
npm run symbolic:research     # clean → experiments → ml → gold → review → publish
```

The research workflow, in order:

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Commands
items.text:
1. `npm run symbolic:clean`: snapshots the current occurrences
   (`warehouse/features/symbolic/occurrences_before_cleaning.parquet`), rebuilds silver with
   the cleaning and writes `cleaning_audit.parquet` and `cleaning_comparison.json`.
2. Archive the experiment results the new run will be compared with:
   `python platform/nlp/symbolic/experiments.py --archive <label>` (copies them to
   `experiments/history/<label>/`; `v2-before-cleaning` is the archive used today).
3. `npm run symbolic:experiments` (and `npm run symbolic:ml` for the published baseline: the
   cleaning changes character offsets and so occurrence ids).
4. `npm run symbolic:review`: ranks the book-centred clusters and writes `review/`.
5. Read `review/representative_passages.parquet` (both sets) and `cluster_keywords.parquet`
   for the clusters at the top of `review/cluster_candidates.parquet`.
6. Edit `platform/nlp/symbolic/reviewed_clusters.json` by hand (see [Human review](#human-review)).
7. `npm run symbolic:gold && npm run symbolic:publish`, then the **Publish to R2** workflow.

No step writes `reviewed_clusters.json`; rerunning everything never overwrites a review.

The ML stage needs PyTorch (CPU) and the packages in `platform/requirements-symbolic.txt`,
which are kept out of `requirements.txt` so CI stays light. Scripts are run by path, like the
rest of `platform/`: `python -m platform…` would collide with Python's own `platform` module.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Commands
items.text:
After publishing, run the **Publish to R2** workflow (Actions) on the branch to upload the
Parquet files; the site reads them from R2 and falls back to its own copy until then.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Corpus
items.text:
**v4: 101 books** in twelve tradition groups (`platform/ingest/symbolic/corpus.json`, one
document per line). v1–v3 used the ten books marked `pilot`.

How the books were chosen and checked:

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Corpus
items.text:
1. **From the catalogue, not from memory.** Candidates were searched per tradition in Project
   Gutenberg's catalogue (`pg_catalog.csv`), preferring complete, independent works: one
   translation per work, no anthology that reprints another chosen book, single files only
   (so Ovid is Howard's complete blank-verse edition and Malory is volume 1).
2. **Against Gutenberg's own record.** For every book the Gutenberg RDF record gave the title,
   the creators with their roles (author, translator, editor, compiler), the language and the
   rights. All 101 are English and "Public domain in the USA." Title, author, translator and
   editor in `corpus.json` come from that record; tradition, culture, region, genre, source
   type and period are curated.
3. **Against the files.** `platform/ingest/symbolic/audit_corpus.py` (after the ingest) checks
   the fields, that each file's own header names the same title in English, the length (at
   least 5,000 words), and duplicated text between books: the share of one book's eight-word
   shingles found in another. It writes `corpus_audit.json` and stops on a duplicate.
   *Sakoontala* (12169) was dropped because 52 % of it is reprinted in *Hindu Literature*
   (13268). Smaller overlaps remain (27 % of the *Mabinogion* is in Bulfinch's *Age of
   Chivalry*, 22 % of *Serbian Folk-lore* in *Hero Tales of the Serbians*); they are handled
   per passage (below).

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Corpus
items.text:
| Tradition group | Books |
|---|---|
| Greek and Roman | 13 |
| Norse and Germanic | 10 |
| Celtic and Arthurian | 10 |
| East Asian | 10 |
| Indigenous North American | 10 |
| European folklore | 10 |
| Slavic and Eastern European | 9 |
| Christian and Biblical | 9 |
| South Asian | 8 |
| Egyptian and Ancient Near East | 6 |
| Finnish and Baltic | 3 |
| Middle Eastern and Persian | 3 |

Source types: 42 translations, 33 folklore collections, 17 retellings, 8 literary works and
one work written in English (Malory). Finnish/Baltic and Middle Eastern/Persian stay small:
Gutenberg has few complete, independent English texts for them, and the corpus does not pad a
group with weak sources to reach a quota.

Every book is read in English. Many are translations or retellings by nineteenth-century
English writers, so "tradition" is partly also "translator"; the validity checks below test
that directly.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Symbol vocabulary
items.text:
Twenty symbols (`platform/seeds/symbolic/symbols.csv`) and their aliases
(`symbol_aliases.csv`): plural forms, and a few near-synonyms kept deliberately narrow
(serpent and viper for snake, flame for fire, gate for door). Nothing is stemmed or lemmatised.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Occurrence extraction
docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Embedding, map and clusters
items.text:
`platform/nlp/symbolic/pipeline.py`:

1. **Sample.** At most 15 occurrences per book and symbol (30 in v1–v3), chosen by occurrence
   id (a hash), so a long book or a common word does not fill the map, leaving out passages
   another book reprints (`duplicate_of` in silver). v4: 21,898 of 72,926 occurrences, 436
   marked as reprints. The pilot: 4,804 of 12,712 after the paratext cleaning.
2. **Embed.** `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, 384 dimensions, normalised, on the CPU.
   No text leaves the machine. The vectors stay in `warehouse/features/` and are never delivered.
3. **Map.** UMAP to 2 dimensions: cosine, `n_neighbors` 15, `min_dist` 0.1, `random_state` 42.
4. **Cluster.** UMAP to 10 dimensions (`min_dist` 0.0), then HDBSCAN from scikit-learn with
   `min_cluster_size` 20, `min_samples` 10. The number of clusters is not set in advance.
5. **Evaluate** and write `run.json` (model, parameters, counts, time) and `evaluation.json`.

The run is deterministic: the same corpus gives the same map and clusters.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Evaluation (current baseline, after the paratext cleaning)
items.text:
| Measure | Value | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| Clusters | 50 | groups HDBSCAN found (43 before the cleaning) |
| Noise | 29 % | points in no cluster (38 %) |
| Trustworthiness (2-D map) | 0.85 | the map mostly keeps each point's neighbours |
| Silhouette (10-D, clustered points) | 0.49 | clusters are reasonably separated (0.51) |
| Median membership probability | 0.99 | clustered points sit firmly in their cluster |
| Largest book's share per cluster | 69 % | clusters mostly hold one book (74 %) |
| Largest symbol's share per cluster | 28 % | clusters mix symbols |

**The main finding so far:** the clusters follow books (their style, era and translator) much
more than symbols. Well-separated clusters are therefore not evidence of shared symbolic
meaning. The page says so next to the map.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Deconfounding experiments
items.text:
`platform/nlp/symbolic/experiments.py` (`npm run symbolic:experiments`) runs the **same
occurrence sample** four ways. The sample is defined once (`pipeline.sample`) and every
`run.json` carries the SHA-256 of its ordered occurrence ids, so it can be checked that all
four used identical points. Embeddings are computed twice (original and masked contexts) and
shared; each variant gets its own UMAP map, 10-D UMAP space and HDBSCAN run with the
pipeline's parameters.

| Experiment | Input to UMAP | Tests |
|---|---|---|
| `baseline` | embeddings of the original contexts | the control; identical to the published atlas |
| `masked` | embeddings of contexts with the matched word replaced by `[SYMBOL]` | does structure survive when the symbol's identity is hidden? |
| `book_centered` | original embeddings minus their book's mean embedding, re-normalised (L2) | do clusters depend less on book and style when what a book's passages share is removed? |
| `masked_book_centered` | both | both at once |

`transforms.py`:

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Deconfounding experiments
items.text:
- `mask_symbol(context, matched_term)` replaces every whole-word, case-insensitive use of the
  matched term ("serpent", not "serpentine"; other aliases are left). A second use in the
  neighbouring sentences is masked too, since it would reveal the symbol.
- `center_by_document(vectors, document_ids)` subtracts each book's mean over the sampled
  occurrences only, then L2-normalises. This removes what a book's passages share on average:
  style, era, translator, but also any theme a book carries throughout. It reduces the book
  signal; it does not remove author, translator or style bias in any strict sense.

Outputs, under `warehouse/features/symbolic/experiments/` (local, not delivered): per
experiment `atlas_projection.parquet`, `evaluation.json`, `run.json`,
`cluster_composition.parquet` and `cluster_representatives.parquet`; and `comparison.json` /
`comparison.parquet`, one row per experiment. The site publishes `experiment-comparison.json`
and `cross-book-clusters.json` (counts, shares and representative ids only).

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Measures
items.text:
Per non-noise cluster (`cluster_composition.parquet`): occurrence count; the number of
distinct books, traditions and symbols; the largest of each and its share; and the
**normalised entropy** of each: Shannon entropy divided by log(K), where K is the number of
categories in the whole experiment (10 books, 7 traditions, 20 symbols). 0 means one category;
1 means spread evenly over all of them. Dividing by the corpus-wide K, not by the categories
present in the cluster, keeps clusters comparable.

A **cross-book cluster** has at least 3 books and no book with more than half of it
(`CROSS_BOOK_MIN_BOOKS = 3`, `CROSS_BOOK_MAX_SHARE = 0.5` in `evaluation.py`).

Per experiment: the means of those shares and entropies, unweighted (each cluster counts
once, `mean_*`) and weighted by cluster size (`weighted_mean_*`); how many clusters have 2, 3
or 4+ books and 2 or 3+ traditions; the cross-book cluster count and the share of all sampled
occurrences that fall in one.

Representatives: for each cluster, the 15 members nearest its centroid in the 10-D clustering
space, ties broken by position; nothing is chosen at random. Each run also keeps its 10-D
clustering space (`cluster_space.parquet`, local only) for the review.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Results before the paratext cleaning (run 2026-10-05, 4,869 occurrences, same sample in all four)
items.text:
Archived in `experiments/history/v2-before-cleaning/`.

| | Baseline | Masked | Book-centred | Both |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clusters | 43 | 51 | 50 | 53 |
| Noise | 38 % | 37 % | 32 % | 37 % |
| Trustworthiness | 0.85 | 0.84 | 0.83 | 0.80 |
| Silhouette | 0.51 | 0.52 | 0.52 | 0.51 |
| Largest book share (mean / weighted) | 0.74 / 0.72 | 0.71 / 0.74 | **0.57 / 0.50** | 0.59 / 0.55 |
| Largest tradition share | 0.80 | 0.82 | **0.64** | 0.67 |
| Largest symbol share | 0.28 | 0.23 | 0.29 | 0.22 |
| Book entropy (normalised) | 0.32 | 0.33 | **0.51** | 0.48 |
| Clusters with 3+ books | 32 | 42 | 44 | 47 |
| Cross-book clusters | 5 | 8 | **24** | 19 |
| Occurrences in cross-book clusters | 7 % | 8 % | **43 %** | 28 % |

What this says:

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Results before the paratext cleaning (run 2026-10-05, 4,869 occurrences, same sample in all four)
items.text:
- **Book-centring reduced book dependence the most**: book share 0.74 → 0.57 (0.72 → 0.50
  weighted), cross-book clusters 5 → 24, holding 43 % of the points, and silhouette did not
  drop. Book identity is a large, removable part of the baseline structure.
- **Masking hid the symbol, not the book**: symbol share fell (0.28 → 0.23) but book share
  barely moved. The clusters were never mainly about the symbol word; they follow the
  surrounding prose.
- **Combining both** sits between: fewer cross-book clusters than book-centring alone. Without
  the word, what is left of a passage after removing the book's mean is weaker.
- **Book effects are reduced, not gone**: even book-centred, a cluster's largest book holds
  57 % on average.
- **A failure mode surfaced**: one of the largest book-centred cross-book clusters is built
  from Bulfinch's glossary and index entries ("Aegisthus, murderer of Agamemnon…"), not from
  narrative. Paratext (indexes, notes, contents) survives the silver cleaning and forms its own
  clusters; it should be cut before the next run. Other cross-book clusters, such as passages
  about death and graves drawn from the Eddas, Hesiod and Bulfinch, look thematic, but no
  cluster has been reviewed by a person and none is named.

No variant is called best: the book-centred map trades a little trustworthiness (0.85 → 0.83)
for much less book dependence, which is what the follow-up question asks for.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Paratext cleaning
items.text:
`platform/nlp/symbolic/cleaning.py`, run in the silver model `int_symbolic_documents` (now a
dbt Python model). The old SQL collapsed every line break before cleaning, which hid the
structure that shows where paratext is; the new cleaning reads the lines first and collapses
white space last. Each rule is its own function and none is one big regular expression:

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Paratext cleaning
items.text:
| Rule | Function | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| Gutenberg header, licence and credit | `strip_gutenberg_boilerplate` | START/END markers; a leading "Produced by …" paragraph |
| Footnotes and transcriber's notes | `remove_footnote_blocks` | bracketed `[Footnote 12: …]` blocks, wherever they stand |
| Tables of contents | `remove_table_of_contents` | a CONTENTS / TABLE OF CONTENTS / LIST OF ILLUSTRATIONS heading, then list-like paragraphs (lines in capitals, numbered, CHAPTER/BOOK/RUNE…, page numbers, indented titles) up to the first paragraph that is not a list |
| Glossaries | `remove_glossary_sections` | a GLOSSARY / VOCABULARY heading **and** entries that look like "Term, …" / "Term. …" (60 % or more) |
| Indexes | `remove_index_sections` | an INDEX heading **and** entries with page numbers (half or more) or glossary-like entries |
| Notes, references, appendices | `remove_editorial_notes` | BIBLIOGRAPHY / REFERENCES anywhere; NOTES, FOOTNOTES, ENDNOTES, APPENDIX, DRAMATIS PERSONAE in the last quarter of a book, or earlier only when their entries look like notes ("[1] …") |
| The document | `clean_document` | all of the above, then white space collapsed |

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Paratext cleaning
items.text:
A heading is a short line on its own with at least two blank lines before it, as Gutenberg sets
section headings. Words alone never trigger anything: "index", "notes" or "contents" in a
sentence are prose. A section runs to the next heading in capitals that is not itself an entry,
or to the end of the book. The rules are conservative: a section heading over prose is kept.

Safeguards: the model raises if a book would lose more than half its text or keep fewer than
5,000 words, and warns above 30 %. Paragraph order is kept. Character offsets are offsets in
the cleaned text, so occurrence ids (hash of book, offset and symbol) stay deterministic for a
cleaning version, but change when the cleaning changes.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Cleaning audit
items.text:
Each row of `int_symbolic_documents` carries its audit: `raw_char_count`, `body_char_count`
(after boilerplate), `clean_char_count`, `removed_char_count`, `removed_share`,
`sections_removed` (kind:heading, JSON), `footnote_blocks_removed`, `cleaning_warnings` and
`cleaning_version`. `cleaning_report.py` writes `warehouse/features/symbolic/cleaning_audit.parquet`
and `cleaning_comparison.json` (occurrences before and after, per book, symbol and tradition).

| Book | Removed | Sections |
|---|---|---|
| Andersen's Fairy Tales | 0.1 % | contents |
| Bulfinch's Mythology | 5.2 % | contents, glossary, 75 footnotes |
| Celtic Fairy Tales | 4.1 % | contents, notes and references |
| The Elder and Younger Eddas | 9.1 % | contents, glossary, 137 footnotes |
| Grimms' Fairy Tales | 0.3 % | contents |
| Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns | 9.0 % | bibliography, endnotes |
| Kalevala | 1.3 % | contents, glossary |
| Myths of the Norsemen | 0.5 % | contents, list of illustrations, notes |
| The Odyssey | 7.6 % | footnotes |
| Paradise Lost | 0.0 % | contents |

Occurrences: 13,168 → 12,712 (456 fewer, 9 of 10 books affected; Paradise Lost unchanged).
The largest losses are in Bulfinch (−207, its glossary), the Eddas (−107) and the Kalevala
(−58); by symbol, river (−55), mother (−41) and tree (−39).

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Post-cleaning experiment
items.text:
All four variants rerun on the cleaned occurrences with unchanged UMAP and HDBSCAN parameters,
so only the cleaning differs (`experiments/post_cleaning_comparison.json`). 4,804 occurrences,
the same sample in all four.

| | Baseline | Masked | Book-centred | Both |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clusters | 43 → 50 | 51 → 40 | 50 → 59 | 53 → 57 |
| Noise | 38 → 29 % | 37 → 30 % | 32 → 36 % | 37 → 40 % |
| Trustworthiness | 0.85 → 0.85 | 0.84 → 0.84 | 0.83 → 0.83 | 0.80 → 0.81 |
| Silhouette | 0.51 → 0.49 | 0.52 → 0.47 | 0.52 → 0.53 | 0.51 → 0.54 |
| Largest book share (mean) | 0.74 → 0.69 | 0.71 → 0.69 | 0.57 → 0.58 | 0.59 → 0.60 |
| Book entropy | 0.32 → 0.36 | 0.33 → 0.35 | 0.51 → 0.48 | 0.48 → 0.46 |
| Cross-book clusters | 5 → 10 | 8 → 9 | 24 → 25 | 19 → 23 |
| Occurrences in them | 7 → 11 % | 8 → 19 % | 43 → 32 % | 28 → 23 % |
| Suspected paratext clusters | 1 → 0 | 2 → 0 | 2 → 0 | 2 → 0 |

What this says, and what it does not:

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Post-cleaning experiment
items.text:
- **The paratext clusters are gone** in every variant, including the two glossary clusters of
  the book-centred run (Bulfinch's, 173 points, which had counted as cross-book; the Eddas', 70).
- **Book-centred cross-book clusters held up** (24 → 25), but their share of passages fell from
  43 % to 32 %: part of the earlier cross-book structure was glossary entries. The aggregate
  improvement claimed before the cleaning was partly paratext.
- **The baseline lost some book dependence** (0.74 → 0.69) once front and back matter, which
  each book has in its own style, were gone.
- Aggregate metrics alone do not show the remaining clusters mean anything; that is what the
  review is for.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Cluster candidate ranking
items.text:
`platform/nlp/symbolic/rank_clusters.py` ranks the book-centred clusters **for review, not for
meaning**. `review_priority_score` (0 to 1) is a weighted mean of documented components:

| Weight | Component |
|---|---|
| 0.25 | book entropy (normalised) |
| 0.20 | tradition entropy (normalised) |
| 0.20 | 1 − largest book share |
| 0.15 | mean HDBSCAN membership probability |
| 0.10 | symbol diversity, min(symbols, 5) / 5 |
| 0.10 | size, min(1, log n / log 200) |

Audit flags never remove a cluster from the results; they set its `review_class`:

- `suspected_paratext`: 20 % or more of its passages read as paratext. A passage is paratext
  when it has a run of glossary entries ("Aegisthus, murderer of Agamemnon"), capitalised
  headwords ("KERLAUG: …"), or two weaker signals together (many capitalised words, page
  references, editorial markers such as "See", "cf.", "vol.", a high share of digits). The 20 %
  is calibrated on the run before cleaning: its two glossary clusters had 31 % and 21 %, every
  narrative cluster at most 9 %.
- `too_small`: fewer than 30 passages. `book_dominated`: not cross-book (one book holds more
  than half, or fewer than three books). `low_membership`: mean membership below 0.5.
- `reject` = paratext or too small, `warning` = book-dominated or low membership, otherwise
  `candidate`.

Today: 59 clusters, **19 candidates**, 22 warnings, 18 set aside (all too small), **0
suspected paratext**, 25 cross-book.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Cluster candidate ranking
docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Human review
items.text:
`platform/nlp/symbolic/reviewed_clusters.json` is edited by hand only:

```json
{
  "experiment": "book_centered",
  "clusters": {
    "17": {
      "fingerprint": "3f2a…",
      "status": "reviewed",
      "label": "Threshold / passage",
      "description": "Contexts involving movement across boundaries, entrances, shores or transitions.",
      "interpretation": "Why this cluster matters, in a few sentences.",
      "confidence": "medium",
      "reviewed_by": "human",
      "notes": "Appears across several books and traditions."
    }
  }
}
```

Statuses: `unreviewed`, `candidate`, `reviewed`, `rejected`. A reviewed entry needs a
fingerprint, label, description and confidence (low, medium, high); `reviews.py` refuses the
file otherwise. Cluster numbers change whenever anything upstream changes, so an entry is
matched to the current run by its **fingerprint** (the hash of the cluster's member ids, in
`cluster_candidates.parquet`), not its number. An entry whose fingerprint matches no current
cluster is reported as stale in `review_summary.json` and ignored, never published under a
cluster it did not read.

Today the file has **no reviewed clusters**: nothing has been labelled yet.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Reviewed labels
items.text:
Only entries with status `reviewed` are published (`reviewed-clusters.json`: cluster id, label,
description, interpretation, confidence, book/tradition/symbol counts, representative ids).
Notes stay private. No label is generated: keywords and any later automatic suggestion stay in
the review artefacts and never become public labels. Unreviewed clusters are "Cluster n".

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Cross-book atlas
items.text:
The page has three views of the same points (`?view=`):

- **Baseline**: the published atlas, coloured by cluster in muted hues on the dark plate.
- **Cross-book**: the book-centred map. Noise is faint, book-bound and rejected clusters are
  grey, cross-book candidates stone, reviewed clusters off-white and labelled on the map, the
  chosen cluster on top; a key beside the map names the three tones. Choosing a cluster (a point or the cluster list) opens its
  panel: name if reviewed, number, review status and audit class, passages, books, traditions,
  symbols, largest book share, book entropy, mean membership, top symbols and traditions and
  representative passages one book at a time; for reviewed clusters also the description,
  confidence and the reviewer's "why this cluster matters".
- **Reviewed**: only reviewed clusters lit; until there are any the page says "No reviewed
  semantic clusters yet."

Under the map, "How the investigation went" tells the steps (question, baseline, problem,
deconfounding, cleaning, review, result) with the numbers from `research-history.json`; the
cluster-quality diagnostics (trustworthiness, silhouette, noise, membership) are under Method.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Delivery
docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Delivery
items.text:
The export reruns the ranking first, so the published review status always matches
`reviewed_clusters.json`. No embedding and no text beyond each point's excerpt is delivered.
It registers the files in `catalog.json` and `delivery.json` with the same rules as
`build_catalog.py`, touching no other entry. Parquet is delivered from R2.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Frontend
items.text:
`frontend/src/symbolic/`: `SymbolicAtlasPage` (route `#symbolic-atlas`, lazy-loaded),
`AtlasCanvas` (canvas, one dot per point, colour by cluster, noise grey, hover and click),
`AtlasSidebar` (symbol, tradition, cluster and noise filters, kept in the address:
`?symbol=snake`, `?tradition=norse`, `?cluster=3`, and the view, `?view=cross-book`),
`ClusterPanel` (a book-centred cluster for review), `ResearchStory` (the investigation step by
step), `ExperimentTable`, `atlasData` (loading through the delivery manifest) and `atlasTypes`.
The review layer is optional: without its files the page is the baseline atlas.

The map's view spans the 0.2–99.8 percentiles of the coordinates; the few points outside it
are drawn as rings at the edge, and the page says how many. No coordinate is changed.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › v4: the expanded corpus (run 2026-10-06)
items.text:
The experiment changes one thing: the corpus, from 10 to 101 books. The symbols, the
extraction, the cleaning, the embedding model and the UMAP and HDBSCAN settings are those of
v3. Two consequences of a larger corpus are handled and stated: the sample cap went from 30 to
15 passages per book and symbol (so 101 books give 21,898 points, not 50,000), and passages one
book reprints from another are left out. The v3 results are archived in
`experiments/history/v3-pilot/` and stay in the research history.

Book-centred (the cross-book view), v3 pilot against v4:

| Measure | v3 (10 books) | v4 (101 books) |
|---|---|---|
| Passages mapped | 4,804 | 21,898 |
| Clusters | 59 | 114 |
| Noise | 36 % | 52 % |
| Largest book's share of a cluster | 58 % | 36 % |
| Clusters over several books | 25 | 87 |
| Passages in them | 32 % | 44 % |
| Silhouette (10-D) | 0.53 | 0.31 |
| Trustworthiness (2-D) | 0.83 | 0.74 |

Baseline (no centring), v4: 130 clusters, 49 % noise, largest book 50 % (69 % in v3).

**What the clusters follow** (`platform/nlp/symbolic/validity.py`, adjusted mutual information
between the cluster labels and each property, 0 = chance):

| Property | Baseline | Book-centred |
|---|---|---|
| Symbol | 0.13 | 0.20 |
| Book | 0.49 | 0.20 |
| English voice (translator or compiler) | 0.45 | 0.18 |
| Tradition | 0.40 | 0.16 |
| Genre | 0.40 | 0.15 |
| Period | 0.24 | 0.09 |
| Source type | 0.21 | 0.08 |

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › v4: the expanded corpus (run 2026-10-06)
items.text:
Book pairs, book-centred (mean similarity of two books' spread over the clusters, 0–1): 0.27
for pairs that share nothing, 0.31 for the same source type or period, 0.34 for the same
tradition, 0.35 for the same genre, 0.36 for the same English voice (14 pairs).

Reading these honestly:

- With more books, a cluster is less often one book: the largest book's share fell from 58 % to
  36 %, and most clusters now span several books.
- Without centring the map still follows the book (AMI 0.49) far more than the symbol (0.13).
  Book-centring brings symbol and book level (0.20 each); it does not make symbol dominant.
- The structure is weaker: half the points are noise and the silhouette fell from 0.53 to 0.31.
  A wider corpus is more varied, and the parameters were not retuned, by design.
- Shared genre, tradition and English voice still make books more alike than books sharing
  nothing. The voice test rests on 14 pairs and is the least certain.
- No v4 cluster has been reviewed. The five v3 labels were written for v3's clusters and do not
  carry over (`reviews.py` matches them by fingerprint); 61 v4 clusters are ranked for review.
- Not measured: literal against symbolic use of a word; that needs a hand-labelled sample.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Embedding models (run 2026-10-07)
items.text:
`python platform/nlp/symbolic/experiments.py --models` embeds the same 21,898 passages with
four sentence-transformers models (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5, intfloat/e5-base-v2
with its `query: ` prefix, thenlper/gte-base) and runs the baseline and book-centred experiments
for each. It writes `experiments/models/<model>/` and `experiments/models/comparison.json`,
published as `model-comparison.json`. The vectors stay local (`embeddings.npy`), so a rerun skips
the slow part.

HDBSCAN's settings were chosen for MiniLM, and bge-base collapses under them to five clusters
(two book-centred), so cluster counts alone cannot compare models. The comparison therefore adds a
measure with no map and no clusters (`evaluation.neighbourhood`): for each passage, the share of
its 10 nearest neighbours (cosine) from the same book, tradition or symbol, next to the share a
random neighbour would have (1 % same book, 5 % same symbol).

Book-centred:

| Model | Neighbours, same book | Neighbours, same symbol | Clusters | Book share | Noise | Embedding |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| all-MiniLM-L6-v2 | 26 % | 26 % | 114 | 36 % | 52 % | 4 min |
| bge-base-en-v1.5 | 22 % | 30 % | 2 | 6 % | 4 % | 21 min |
| e5-base-v2 | 24 % | 30 % | 88 | 26 % | 66 % | 22 min |
| gte-base | 25 % | 31 % | 98 | 28 % | 61 % | 20 min |

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Embedding models (run 2026-10-07)
items.text:
- Every larger model moves the same way: fewer same-book neighbours, about four points more
  same-symbol ones. The step is small next to the book and tradition effect.
- The symbol word is still in each passage, so part of "same symbol" is the word itself.
- The atlas keeps all-MiniLM-L6-v2. A larger model would need new HDBSCAN settings, and those
  should change only after the clusters have been reviewed.
- Centring by translator was not run: only three translators have more than one book in the
  corpus, so it would be almost the same as centring by book.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Limitations
items.text:
- Symbol matching is lexicon-based: "fire" in "fire-sword" and "gate" as a door both count, and
  a word used literally counts like one used symbolically.
- A context is not a symbolic meaning; the embedding sees the topic and style of a passage.
- Clusters are exploratory, not ground truth, and their ids carry no meaning. Cross-book
  clusters are not archetypes, and nothing here shows a meaning is universal across cultures.
- The paratext rules are heuristics: some paratext may survive and some short headings over
  narrative may go; the audit records every removal so either can be checked.
- The review priority is a heuristic for where to spend a reader's time, not a measure of
  meaning, and its weights are a choice.
- The corpus is 101 English books chosen from one archive; another selection gives another
  map, and Gutenberg's holdings over-represent nineteenth-century English translators and
  collectors.
- UMAP distorts the high-dimensional geometry; distances between far-apart groups on the map
  mean little.
- HDBSCAN leaves many points as noise by design.

items.title: docs/symbolic-atlas.md › Future work
items.text:
- Review the top candidates by hand (`review/representative_passages.parquet`) and record the
  outcome in `reviewed_clusters.json`, rejections included.
- Tune UMAP and HDBSCAN only after the review, so the effect of cleaner text stays isolated.
- Try per-symbol analyses within one book.
- Retune HDBSCAN per embedding model after the review, then compare the models' clusters too.
- More books per tradition, and books in their original languages with a multilingual model.

items.title: docs/taxes.md › Tax data and calculation checks
items.text:
The tax pipeline delivers the following data from official sources. The former
standalone tax page and calculator are retired; `#taxes` leads to the budget report, `#politik-budget`.
The calculation core and its source-based tests remain available locally.

| Part | Source | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| Tax revenue per tax type, Sweden and every OECD country | OECD Revenue Statistics (general government) | 1965 to the latest year, share of GDP and national currency |
| Tax on a salary by country, household and wage level | OECD Taxing Wages | 2000 to the latest year |
| Local income tax, burial and church fee per parish | Skatteverket open data | every year Skatteverket publishes |
| The rules of the calculator | Skatteverket, SKV 433 and *Belopp och procentsatser* | income year 2026 |

items.title: docs/taxes.md › The calculator
items.text:
`frontend/src/taxes/calculator.ts` is the implementation used by
`frontend/tests/unit/tax-calculator.test.ts`. The rules for each year are in
`frontend/src/taxes/rules.ts`, with a source for every amount.

**What it computes**
- Final annual tax on:
  - salary
  - pension
  - other pension-qualifying benefits (unemployment, parental and sickness benefit)
  - sickness and activity compensation
  - the profit of a sole proprietorship, after self-employment contributions
  - interest and dividends
  - capital gains and losses
  - ISK and capital insurance (deemed income)
  - interest paid, e.g. a mortgage (the capital-deficit reduction)
  - the property fee of a small house
- The basic allowance, including the raised allowance from 66.
- The in-work tax credit, for people under and over 66.
- The pension contribution and its reduction.
- The earned-income reduction and the public service fee.
- What the employer pays on top, with the reduced rates by age and the youth reduction of 2026, and the resulting tax wedge.

**What it leaves out**
- VAT and excise duties.
- Deductions (travel to work, double housing).
- The property-fee cap for pensioners.
- Foreign income.
- Tax-free benefits such as child benefit.

**Tested against Skatteverket.** Every row of the 2026 monthly withholding tables (tables 29–42, all six columns, 40,404 cases) gives the same tax to the krona. So do the worked examples in SKV 433. The table fixture is regenerated by `export_taxes.py`.

items.title: docs/taxes.md › The calculator
items.text: **A new income year.** Add its entry to `rules.ts` from Skatteverket's SKV 433 and *Belopp och procentsatser*. Then run `npm run taxes`, which fetches the new year's tables, and run `npm run test:unit`. The test fails until the rules match the tables.

items.title: docs/taxes.md › Every year since 2006
items.text:
The rules are data per income year (`frontend/src/taxes/rules.ts`): the basic allowance, the
higher allowance and the in-work credit as piecewise schedules in price base amounts, the state
tax brackets, the ages for older people, the reductions each year had, and the amounts the
tables do not show (ISK, property fee, social contributions by birth year and month, VAT).
Every year from 2016 matches Skatteverket's monthly withholding tables to the krona
(`frontend/tests/unit/tax-calculator.test.ts`). There are no tables as open data before 2016,
so 2006–2015 are tested against the worked examples in SKV 433 for 2010 and 2013 (allowances
and in-work credit). The sources per year:

items.title: docs/taxes.md › Every year since 2006
items.text:
| Years | Source |
|---|---|
| 2006 | No in-work credit, no higher allowance at 65; state property tax 1 % without a cap |
| 2007–2010 | The bills for each step of the in-work credit and the pensioners' allowance (prop. 2006/07:1, 2007/08:22, 2008/09:38, 2008/09:39, 2009/10:29, 2009/10:42); at 65 or over in 2007–2008 the credit less the basic allowance, as for younger people |
| 2011–2015 | The budget bills, and SKV 433 2013 |
| 2016, 2020–2026 | Skatteverket, Teknisk beskrivning SKV 433 |
| 2017 | 2016's rules with 2017's amounts, confirmed by the tables |
| 2018 | Prop. 2017/18:1 (förhöjt grundavdrag), SKV 433 bilaga 3 2018 (in-work credit) |
| 2019 | Bet. 2018/19:FiU1, reservation 5 (M, KD): the law text adopted |
| All years | Skatteverket, Belopp och procent (2006–2026); Kommunal fastighetsavgift 2008–2026 |

Not modelled before 2016: the wealth tax (abolished 2007), and ISK before it began in 2012.

The tables up to 2019 rounded municipal tax and fees to the nearest krona; up to 2017 they
assumed 1.2 points of burial and church fee. The temporary work income reduction of 2021–2022
(SFS 2021:930) is given in the final tax only, so the calculator has it and the tables do not.

items.title: docs/taxes.md › Decisions and you
items.text:
`platform/seeds/taxes/tax_decisions.csv` names each Riksdag decision that changed a tax since
2007: the part of the rules it changed, the bill and section, the committee report, and whether
it came from the government, the committee's own proposal or a reservation. dbt ties each to
the first substantive roll call of its report (`fct_tax_decision_vote`) and to the studies its
proposal was prepared in (`fct_tax_decision_study`). Fuel decisions carry the change per litre
and the months it applied, from each bill.

The household estimate uses SCB's household budget survey (HUT 2021): spending per group, prices
including VAT, VAT = spending × rate / (100 + rate), only groups with one clear rate. It is a
floor. The 2026 food VAT cut assumes full pass-through.

items.title: docs/taxes.md › Reading the comparisons
items.text:
- The **tax wedge** is income tax plus employee and employer contributions, less cash benefits, as a share of labour cost.
  - The OECD computes it at 67, 100 and 167 % of each country's own average wage.
  - Countries are therefore compared at the same place in their own wage scale, not at the same salary in kronor.
- **Revenue as a share of GDP** is tax *collected*, not tax *rates*.
  - It depends on what the tax pays for: pensions and health care are tax-financed in Sweden and partly private elsewhere.
  - It also depends on the size of the economy.

items.title: docs/taxes.md › Running
items.text:
```bash
npm run taxes        # python platform/pipeline.py run taxes: fetch, dbt build, export
npm run test:unit    # the calculator against Skatteverket's tables
```

The dbt step selects `+tag:taxes`, so it also builds the parliament models the tax decisions
read: bills, studies, reports and roll calls. Before it fetches anything,
`platform/ingest/taxes/require_parliament.py` checks that the parliament raw files have
complete, hash-verified checkpoints, and stops with an upstream error if a session is
unfinished or a file is missing. On an empty machine, run `python platform/pipeline.py pull
parliament` or `run parliament` first. An existing gold table is not accepted in their place.

items.title: docs/thesis-evidence-review.md › Motsägelser och öppna begränsningar
items.text:
- HDBSCAN-svepet: tabell 4.2.3 på s. 29 placerar `0,443` under brus och

  `27,7 %` under Davies-Bouldin för vald rad. Dessa kolumner kan inte användas som

  ett sammanhängande svepresultat. Brus 27,7 % stöds separat av tabell 4.2.4,

  diskussionen på s. 38 och figurhuvudet på s. 42.

- Domänexpansion: s. 15, 28 och 37 kallar ökningen i bästa klustrets

  PRB-kopplingsgrad från 36,1 % till 52,4 % isolerad. Tabell 4.2.2 visar dock olika

  populationer, 17 757 respektive 16 811, och olika K-means-antal, 60 respektive 81.

  Portfolion beskriver expansionen utan att tillskriva den en isolerad vinst på

  16 procentenheter. Bästa klustrets värde är inte hela modellens träffsäkerhet.

- Kandidater och artefakter: s. 32 beskriver tre ghost clusters som exkluderade,

  medan s. 33 listar fyra med 291 ärenden i kandidattaxonomin. C68 återkommer som

  verksamhetskandidat på s. 34 och 38 trots artefaktklassning på s. 32. Uppgiften

  om 54 aktionsbara kluster/2 260 ärenden på s. 33 går inte att förena med tabellen

  och sammanfattningens 12/650 på s. 36. De senare återges som den delmängd

  arbetet lyfter fram, utan påstående om slutligt godkänd kandidatlista.

- XGBoost: tabell 4.2.10 på s. 35 anger ROC-AUC 0,882, PR-AUC 0,426,

  precision 0,26, recall 0,58 och F1 0,36. Brödtexten på samma sida anger 0,897,

  tidsuppdelning och skydd mot informationsläckage redovisas inte tillräckligt för

items.text:
att bedöma oberoende generalisering. Portfolion beskriver kontrollens syfte

  utan att välja ett entydigt prestandavärde eller kalla den ett facit för rotorsaker.

- Slutlig textinput: s. 22, 25 och 27 inkluderar konversationer i beskrivningen

  av förberedda fält. Receptet på s. 28 listar bara ämne, analys och beskrivning.

  Exakt användning av konversationsloggar i slutkörningen lämnas öppen.

- Tid och reproducerbarhet: s. 13 och 18 anger slutdatum 2026-04-14, medan

  årstabellen på s. 20 anger 2026-04-22. Portfolion använder intervallet

  2020-2026. UMAP-seeds, fullständig konfiguration, urvalsorsaker från 19 847

  till 16 811 och oberoende seed-/urvalsstabilitet är inte fullt redovisade.

- Förslag är inte uppmätta resultat: borttagning av platshållartokens, större

  domänordlista, lokal språkmodell och intervjuer föreslås på s. 39. Deras effekt

  har inte verifierats här. Den tidigare startsidetexten om ett fel som hanterats

  i tre år ersätts med den aggregerade kandidatbeskrivningen; s. 38 dokumenterar

  liknande symptom över 2021-2024 men fastställer inte en gemensam rotorsak.

items.title: docs/thesis-evidence-review.md › Utökning av ISO-resultat och Education
items.text:
Thesis-sidan har ett eget navigerbart avsnitt om generell datakvalitet, före
modellutvärderingen. Det förklarar de fem valda dimensionerna och skiljer giltiga
systemvärden från innehåll som går att använda för analys:

- Fullständighet: lösningsfältets 82,2 % rå fyllnad och 3,8 % manuell fyllnad,
  samt analysfältets 4,2 % (PDF-s. 19-20, 27).
- Exakthet: symptom kontra teknisk orsak, grova 15/50 kategorier och avsaknad
  av oberoende facit per ärende (PDF-s. 21-22).
- Konsistens: 100 % giltiga status-/prioritetsvärden följer systemtvång och
  fastställer inte kvaliteten i agenternas bedömningar (PDF-s. 23).
- Unikhet: 92,8 % icke-dubbletter enligt källsystemets tidsfönster och
  ämnesradsdetektering; 82,8 % år 2021 och 89,8 % år 2025 (PDF-s. 23-24).
- Spårbarhet: 5,1 % problemkoppling över perioden och 15,7 % under delåret 2026. Avsaknad av registrerad länk är inte avsaknad av känt fel (PDF-s. 24-25).
- Förändring över tid: klassificeringsfältens 99,9 % fyllnad år 2026 och
  analysfältets skilda årsandelar (PDF-s. 20). Detta är ett perspektiv på de fem
  dimensionerna, inte en sjätte utvärderad ISO-dimension.

items.title: docs/thesis-evidence-review.md › Utökning av ISO-resultat och Education
items.text:
Education återger klustringsresultat, långvariga symptom, ISO-mätning,
modelljämförelse och teknikstack. Dokumentation och processmognad beskrivs som
en huvudbegränsning i fallstudien, utan att avfärda modellens begränsningar.
Formuleringen om genomförda verksamhetsintervjuer införs inte: PDF-s. 12 anger
att intervjuerna exkluderades och s. 39 föreslår dem som framtida validering.
